name: Rosen Method Bodywork

card.summary: A gentle-touch and conversation-based bodywork that aims to release chronic muscular tension and ease stress, which people hope will show in posture, face and general well-being.
card.aka: Rosen Method; Rosen bodywork; Rosen Method Movement (related)
card.note: Complementary therapy; research is small-scale and mostly self-reported.

quick.overview:
Rosen Method Bodywork is a complementary therapy developed by physical therapist Marion Rosen. A practitioner uses light, listening touch and brief verbal prompts while the client lies on a table, to draw attention to areas of tension, held breath and emotion.

Clients seek it for stress, chronic pain, body awareness and personal growth. For appearance, the connection is indirect: practitioners say softening chronic holding patterns can change posture, expression and the way someone carries themselves.
quick.how: Sessions are typically one-to-one on a massage table, with the practitioner observing breathing and muscle tone and sometimes inviting the client to speak about what they notice. A companion practice, Rosen Method Movement, is taught as group classes of gentle, flowing movement to music.
quick.risks: The method uses light touch and is not manipulative; adverse effects are not prominent in the literature. Practitioners note that emotions can surface during sessions. Quackwatch has classed it among unnaturalistic methods, and larger controlled trials are lacking.

lead: Rosen Method Bodywork is a form of touch and words-based bodywork developed by Marion Rosen (1914-2012), a physical therapist who trained with Lucy Heyer, a student of Elsa Gindler. Practitioners use gentle contact and verbal prompts to help clients notice tension, breathing and feelings, with the stated aim of releasing chronic muscular holding.[1][2]

People use it for stress, pain and self-awareness. Within an appearance context, practitioners suggest that softer breathing and less habitual tension can show up as more relaxed posture and facial expression, an indirect route to looking more at ease.

Rosen began formal training in 1980 and the Rosen Institute was set up in Berkeley in 1983 to certify practitioners; a Rosen Method Movement program was added later.[1][3] Published research is small: a survey of 53 Swedish clients and a pilot study of five people with chronic low back pain.[4][5]

chain: Light touch and verbal prompts highlight tension and breath
angle.text: Clients use Rosen Method to reduce stress and body tension; practitioners say this can change posture and the look of the face and body. Reported benefits are mostly about well-being rather than appearance.

infobox: One-to-one touch and talk; group movement classes

paras: Clients lie on a table while the practitioner observes the body and gives light, attentive touch. Rather than manipulating tissue, the practitioner invites awareness of sensations, breath and feelings, and may ask simple questions.[1][2] Practitioners hold that chronic muscular tension, especially around the diaphragm, relates to suppressed emotion.[2]

Rosen worked as a physical therapist in the San Francisco Bay Area from the 1940s and noticed that some chronic tension did not respond to standard therapy. She combined her training with the listening-touch approach she had learned from Heyer.[1][3] She trained apprentices from the 1970s, started a professional training program in 1980 and co-founded the Rosen Institute in 1983.[1][3] Wikipedia notes affiliates in 16 countries.[2]

A 2009 exploratory survey of 53 Swedish clients found that most reported the therapy helped them to a high or very high degree, describing benefits in psychological health, physical health, mind-body awareness, personal growth and self-initiated life changes.[4]

A 2013 pilot study followed five adults with chronic low back pain through 16 weekly sessions; all reported reductions in pain and/or disability, with significant reductions in pain and fatigue and gains in emotional state and sense of control, despite large day-to-day variation.[5] A 2007 study of 'clinical holistic medicine' for sexual functioning used bodywork inspired by the Rosen method together with psychotherapy.[6]
Wikipedia notes that interoception research is not specific to Rosen Method, and Quackwatch classifies the method as unnaturalistic.[2]

timeline.event: First professional Rosen training program in Berkeley.[1][3]
